A private network that isn't real

In a real private network there is a dedicated link between two points: nobody else sees what goes through it. But it is expensive, because the provider reserves physical resources exclusively.

A VPN (virtual private network) achieves the same thing virtually: over a public network (the Internet) a tunnel is established, a virtual circuit through which information travels secure and encrypted, as if it were a private network.
VPN = my private network, built virtually on top of a public network.

• Remote access: a user connects to their office and uses the central resources as if they were on that network. It is usually software that connects to the tunnel gateway (a public IP); it is a proprietary solution.
  • Site to site (LAN to LAN): two networks are joined as if by a real circuit, which is actually virtual.

The protocols are distinguished by the layer they work at; IPSec is the current standard.

IPSec is a suite of protocols and configuration options. It was designed to protect IPv6 communications and later ported to IPv4, where it is most used. It offers two modes.

In transport mode it takes the transport layer PDU and encrypts it when it reaches the network layer. One host encrypts it and the other decrypts it.

It protects communication between two hosts: the IP header still shows who is talking.
Transport mode: the only thing encrypted is the transport PDU, wrapped between an IPSec header and trailer. The original IP header stays in front, in plain view, with the addresses of both hosts.

In tunnel mode the hosts don't talk to each other; two gateways do, encrypting all the traffic that goes from one side to the other.

A datagram with source Z and destination T is fully encrypted, header included, and encapsulated inside another IP datagram that carries the gateways' addresses.

Anyone watching the traffic on the Internet sees the conversation between the gateways, not between the hosts that are actually taking part.
Tunnel mode: an encrypted IP datagram, encapsulated inside another and sent.

Tunnel mode: the entire original datagram (IP header with Z and T + transport PDU) becomes the encrypted payload. In front goes a new IP header, with source and destination at the gateways at each end.

IPSec has two protocol variants:

  • AH (Authentication Header): guarantees that the message comes from who it claims to be and that it was not altered. But it does not encrypt: there is no confidentiality.
  • ESP: in addition to authenticity and integrity, it guarantees confidentiality, because it encrypts the data.
AH = authenticity + integrity. ESP = the same + confidentiality.

In AH the authentication digest goes inside the AH header itself and the payload stays readable. In ESP the payload and the trailer are encrypted; authentication covers from the ESP header to the trailer, and the digest travels at the end.
Two private LANs separated by the Internet

We have the LAN 192.168.1.0 and the branch office 192.168.2.0. Routers H and Y reach the Internet with a public IP.

Direct communication is impossible: on the Internet private addresses are not valid.

Pointing at the router's public IP doesn't work either: it is a one-to-many relationship (all the stations go out through that single address), so you can't specifically reach 192.168.2.15 from 192.168.1.100.
The tunnel is the closest thing to a direct link between the two routers.
The 192.168.x.x addresses are private: they work inside each LAN, but no Internet router knows how to reach them.

Each router must be told where the tunnel ends (the peer) and agree on identical parameters on both sides:

  • An encryption protocol (3DES).
  • A hashing method for integrity (SHA).
  • A pre-shared key (PSK): the same private key at both ends. Certificates can also be used.

This initial configuration is the IKE (Internet Key Exchange) policy, the standard protocol for key exchange.

Phase 2 describes what goes inside the tunnel:

  • transform-set: encryption and hash algorithm (the same on both sides).
  • access-list: the traffic descriptor. Cisco's wildcard is the inverse of the mask: 255.255.255.0 → 0.0.0.255.
  • crypto map: ties together the peer, the access list, and the transform-set; there can be several tunnels.

Finally, the crypto map is applied to the interface that faces the Internet.

crypto ipsec transform-set ESP-3DES-SHA esp-3des esp-sha-hmac
access-list 102 permit ip 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 192.168.2.0 0.0.0.255
crypto map IPSEC 20 ipsec-isakmp
  set peer 192.168.3.1
  match address 102
  set transform-set ESP-3DES-SHA
interface fastEthernet 0/0
  crypto map IPSEC

A sends to 192.168.2.15 and the packet goes to its default gateway. When it crosses the outgoing interface it meets the crypto map and its access list.

The entries (ACEs) are evaluated in order: when one matches, the packet is accepted, encrypted and sent through the tunnel.

If it matches none, it falls into the implicit deny any any at the end and does not enter the tunnel. The other router has the same ACL with local and remote swapped.
In an ACL, everything that is not explicitly permitted is denied.
implicit deny any any: not tunneled
VPN and IPSec at a glance

• VPN: a tunnel over a public network instead of a dedicated link.
  • Types: remote access and site to site.
  • IPSec transport (host to host) or tunnel (between gateways, with the whole datagram encapsulated).
  • AH does not encrypt; ESP does.
  • Phase 1 (IKE): encryption, hash, PSK, and peer. Phase 2: transform-set, access list, and crypto map.
